title: UserPart
description: A user-authored custom part as persisted in a project file (and later a user-local library). It is a BLACK BOX drawn from a pin spec — deliberately NOT a full catalog Definition: a built-in primitive_device (see definition.schema.json) must declare its internal composition (what it is physically built from), which a custom part does not have yet. Faking one to pass the definition schema would violate the anti-placeholder rule. So a user part gets its own schema, validated with the same engine + strictness the catalog uses; when the user later gives it real internals/behaviours it can graduate to definition.schema.json. Values are the user's own, so (per OBJECT-MODEL.md §12, origin project/user_local) no provenance is required — but everything is typed and unit-valid. NOTE: the runtime loader (user-part-validate.ts) enforces two extra rules JSON Schema can't express, both in the stricter/safe direction, so it may reject a part this schema accepts: (1) pin ids must be UNIQUE within the part (JSON Schema's uniqueItems can't key on a field), and (2) a parameter amount must be FINITE (an overflow literal like 1e400 parses to Infinity, which is a valid JSON number but poisons downstream math).

id.description: The definition id — the slug of the name; lowercase alphanumerics + underscores, no leading/trailing underscore. Unique; must not collide with a built-in id (enforced at registration, not here).

designatorPrefix.description: The reference-designator letters — U for a chip, J for a connector, etc.

footprintId.description: The board package this part lands on (a BUILTIN_FOOTPRINTS id); pins map to its pads in declaration order. Absent ⇒ no footprint yet, so the part stays off the board.

pins.description: The connection points. Each becomes a wire handle + a terminal name.

behavesAs.description: Optional REAL, simulatable behaviour (slice 4b): the part behaves as a built-in device so the solver runs that device's real physics. `definition` is the built-in device id (e.g. 'resistor'); `terminals` maps each of that device's terminal names to one of this part's pin ids. The runtime validator additionally checks every mapped pin id actually exists on the part.

allOf.$comment: The TOP level must expose at least one port (= pin); a NESTED block may have zero ports (a sub-circuit grouped with no boundary wires is legal block data).

internal.description: Optional REAL internal circuit (slice 4b Model B): the part is built from a whole sub-circuit of real parts, in the solve-core block shape (name/origin/nodes/edges/ports). Each top-level port id must equal one of this part's pin ids 1:1 (a runtime-validator rule JSON Schema can't express). Mutually exclusive with behavesAs (enforced below).

parameters.description: Optional default values — the user's own rough-but-typed scalars (amount + unit). No provenance required at project/user_local origin.

not.$comment: A part simulates ONE way — as a single device (behavesAs) or as its internal circuit (internal), never both.

blockCore.description: The solve core of an internal circuit — the same shape a canvas circuit block flattens from: the real parts (nodes), the wires between them (edges, with their drawn geometry so inner wire lengths stay physically real), and the ports that expose internal terminals. Presentation extras a canvas block can carry (display faces, gate symbols, pin drive marks) are deliberately not persisted here.
